props.title: God Told Me To

sections.content: Larry Cohen's disturbing God Told Me To revolutionized religious horror by blending cosmic terror with gritty NYC police procedural. The film follows Catholic detective Peter Nicholas investigating a series of murders where killers calmly claim divine instruction. Cohen's guerrilla filmmaking captures authentic 1970s New York decay, while the story spirals from street-level violence into alien messiahs and virgin births. It prefigured later religious-conspiracy films like The Seventh Sign (1988) and Stigmata (1999), but with a raw urgency those polished productions lack.

sections.content: Cohen's film emerged during a vital period of religious horror that included The Omen (1976) and The Exorcist (1973). But while those films reinforced traditional good-vs-evil dynamics, God Told Me To deliberately muddles divine and demonic imagery. The film's climactic revelation about alien intervention feels remarkably prescient of later UFO cult movements and Heaven's Gate. Cohen's signature blend of exploitation thrills and social commentary reached its apex here.

The film's influence extends beyond horror into police procedurals dealing with religious violence, like Se7en (1995) and True Detective Season 1 (2014). Tony Lo Bianco's tortured Catholic cop character established a template for detectives whose faith complicates their investigations. The documentary-style shooting of New York, including footage captured during actual St. Patrick's Day parades, created a verite style that horror films still emulate. sections.content: The film's ambitious mixing of genres opened doors for later religious-themed horror that refused simple answers. The First Power (1990) and Fallen (1998) borrowed its police procedural framework while adding supernatural elements. Meanwhile, the cosmic horror aspects influenced everything from Prince of Darkness (1987) to Event Horizon (1997). Even found-footage films like The Last Exorcism (2010) echo Cohen's pseudo-documentary approach to faith-based terror.
